There is nothing to push: the leaderboard fills itself, but only from runs on the **practice** set. What I ran was the **sandbox**, which has no leaderboard.

**Where we are on the leaderboard:** rank 8 of 21, at 52.4 points; first place is 73.5. Our best per case ranges from 0.23 (P11) to 0.86 (P01, P04). The team has 162 of 200 practice sessions left until the quota frees up on 11 Oct at 12:47 UTC.

**The three places you can play:**

| Where | Cases | Opponent | Leaderboard | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `arena-sim` (local) | simulator cases | one scripted supplier | no | free |
| sandbox (on the arena) | 2 demo cases, D01 and D02 | real supplier bots | no | free |
| practice (on the arena) | 10 hosted cases, P01–P18 | real supplier bots | **yes** | 10 sessions per full run |

So my two runs were not local and not on 10 cases. They were against the real bots, on the two demo cases only.

**How a result gets onto the leaderboard:** run a strategy on practice, for example `uv run negotiator run --set practice --strategy lowball`. The arena scores each case, and your best score per case counts. A worse run never lowers your standing; a better one raises it at once. `uv run negotiator board` shows the table.

**Why I said 30 minutes:** the 60 seconds is the limit for each of our replies, not for a case.
- A case runs up to 10 rounds, and the supplier can take up to a minute per reply. D02 took 117 and 175 seconds in my two runs.
- I had planned 7 strategies × 3 repetitions = 21 runs, because a single run is noisy.
- The key allows 10 open sessions, and I held to 3 runs at a time to leave room for the practice run that was going on the same key.
- That makes about 9 batches of roughly 3 minutes each.

One pass of all 7 strategies without repetitions would be about 6 minutes: 14 sessions don't fit under the limit of 10, so it takes two batches.

**What I'd do:** keep screening the remaining tactics on the sandbox for free, then spend 10 practice sessions only on a strategy that beats baseline there. The leaderboard's weakest cases for us (P11, P18, P02, P08) are worth more attention than these tone experiments; there's 40+ points of headroom in those four alone.

Do you want me to put `lowball` on practice now (10 sessions, about 3–5 minutes), or screen `trade` and `shelby` on the sandbox first?

**Afternoon, tomorrow.** 11 Oct 12:47 UTC is 15:47 on your machine's clock (EEST), or 14:47 German time (CEST).

That matters more than it sounds: the code freeze and the Live Final are Sunday at 12:00, so the quota starts freeing up only after the final. The quota is rolling, so each session frees up 24 hours after it was used, and our first ones were used this afternoon. In practice, the **162 practice sessions left are all we get before the freeze**. That is 16 full practice runs of 10 cases, shared by the whole team.

**The logic of testing follows from that budget:**

1. **Simulator (free, seconds).** Does the code work at all: messages valid, case closes, no crash. It says nothing about score.
2. **Sandbox (free, about 3 minutes).** Does the idea help against real bots? Two demo cases only, so it is a filter: drop what clearly hurts (like `budget` on D02), keep what looks equal or better. Repeat a promising one 2–3 times, because the same strategy can swing by 0.1 between runs.
3. **Practice (10 sessions per run, the scarce resource).** Only strategies that survived the sandbox go here. This is the only place that shows the 10 real case types and the only one that moves the leaderboard. Since only the best score per case counts, a run can't hurt our rank; it only costs quota.
4. **Read the replays of the worst cases.** After a practice run, the arena shows the supplier's reasons per round. That is where the real gains are: we score 0.23–0.31 on P11, P18, P02 and P08, while a tone or anchor tweak moves a case by a few points.
5. **Keep one full practice run for Sunday morning.** The brief asks for a rehearsal of the final setup (all cases in parallel, well inside 8 minutes) before the freeze.

A reasonable split of the 162: about 10 for the Sunday rehearsal, most of the rest for whichever strategy is the final candidate and for fixing the four weak cases, and only one run each for experiments that passed the sandbox.

Since someone else is also spending from the same key (38 used so far, 27 of them in the last hour), it's worth agreeing with them who uses how many.

content.text:
Started in the background: all eight strategies that need no LLM (baseline, tactical, lowball, budget, questions, polite, shelby, trade), three repetitions each, four runs at a time. It costs no tokens and no practice sessions and should take about 20 minutes. It pauses between batches if a practice run is going on this machine. I left out `llm` because it spends model tokens.

**How accurate is the sandbox?** Good as a filter, poor as a predictor.

- **What it gets right:** it runs the same arena, rules and scoring against real supplier bots. If a tactic makes a bot dig in or walk on the sandbox, that reaction is real.
- **It is narrow:** two cases and three demo suppliers. Practice has 10 cases across more types (renewal, bundle, raw material, capacity, quality), with suppliers whose history is in the data package. The demo suppliers have almost no history, so anything that relies on reading the supplier barely gets exercised.
- **It does not predict the practice score:** our own numbers show this. The `llm` strategy averaged about 0.60 on the sandbox, but our best-per-case average on practice is 0.52, with cases ranging from 0.23 to 0.86.
- **It is noisy:** only two cases, and the bots answer differently each time. The same strategy has swung by about 0.1 on one case between runs, which is why I'm running three repetitions.

So read the sandbox results as "this tactic hurts", "no visible difference" or "worth a practice run", not as a score forecast. I'll write up the records and a comparison table when the runs finish.
